As a result, they may create abstract and incorrect relationships between ETo and weather data or between ETo and ground-measurements of reference ET that may not have the appropriate structures, accuracies and sensitivities. Good quality assessment and quality control (QAQC) is fundamental to the process. The QAQC step requires overview, correction and concurrence by a knowledgeable human. These guidelines make it clear that it is best to remain with the use of a physics-based reference equation, the FAO-Penman-Monteith equation, and make best estimates for missing weather data, rather than to employ an AI engine that may not adhere to all physical laws that govern ET. The result of the latter process can be the production of tangential errors that violate physical principles. text: The evaporation rate from pans filled with water is easily obtained. In the absence of rain, the amount of water evaporated during a period (mm day-1) corresponds with the decrease in water depth in that period. Pans provide a measurement of the integrated effect of radiation, wind, temperature and humidity on the evaporation from an open water surface. Although the pan responds in a similar fashion to the same climatic factors affecting crop transpiration, several factors produce significant differences in loss of water from a water surface and from a cropped surface. The reflection of solar radiation from water in the shallow pan might be different from the assumed 23 percent for the grass reference surface. Storage of heat within the pan can be appreciable and may cause significant evaporation during the night while most crops transpire only during the daytime. There are also differences in turbulence, temperature and humidity of the air immediately above the respective surfaces. Heat transfer through the sides of the pan occurs and affects the energy balance. Notwithstanding the difference between pan-evaporation and the evapotranspiration of cropped surfaces, the use of pans t

text: The Class A Evaporation pan is circular, 120.7 cm in diameter and 25 cm deep. It is made of galvanized iron (22 gauge) or Monel metal (0.8 mm). The pan is mounted on a wooden open frame platform which is 15 cm above ground level. The soil is built up to within 5 cm of the bottom of the pan. The pan must be level. It is filled with water to 5 cm below the rim, and the water level should not be allowed to drop to more than 7.5 cm below the rim. The water should be regularly renewed, at least weekly, to eliminate extreme turbidity. The pan, if galvanized, is painted annually with aluminum paint. Screens over the pan are not a standard requirement and should preferably not be used. Pans should be protected by fences to keep animals from drinking. The site should preferably be under grass, 20 by 20 m (at least 15 by 15), open on all sides to permit free circulation of the air. It is preferable that stations be located in the centre or on the leeward side of large cropped fields. Pan readings are taken daily in the early morning at the same time that precipitation is measured. Measurements are made in a stilling well that is situated in the pan near one edge. text: The Colorado sunken pan is 92 cm (3 ft) square and 46 cm (18 in) deep, made of 3 mm thick iron, placed in the ground with the rim 5 cm (2 in) above the soil level. The water level is maintained at or slightly below ground level, i.e. 5-7.5 cm below the rim. Measurements are taken similarly to those for the Class A pan. chapter: Chapter 5 — Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement
locator: Chapter 5 — Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement
text: This chapter outlines the crop coefficient (Kc) approach for calculating the crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc). The standard conditions refer to crops grown in large fields under excellent agronomic and soil water conditions. The crop evapotranspiration differs distinctly from the reference evapotranspiration (ETo) as the ground cover, canopy properties and aerodynamic resistance of the crop are different from grass. The effects of characteristics that distinguish field crops from grass are integrated into the crop coefficient. In the crop coefficient approach, crop evapotranspiration is calculated by multiplying ETo by Kc. Differences in evaporation and transpiration between field crops and the reference grass surface can be integrated into a single crop coefficient (Kc) or separated into two coefficients: a basal crop (Kcb) and a soil evaporation coefficient (Ke), i.e. Kc = Kcb + Ke. The approach to follow should be selected as a function of the purpose of the calculation, the accuracy required and the data available. A brief review of ETc measurement using ground and remote observations and sensors is added.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement
locator: Chapter 5 — Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement — Calculation Procedures
text: The evapotranspiration rate from a cropped surface can be directly measured by the mass transfer or the energy balance method. It can also be derived from studies of the soil water balance determined from cropped fields or from lysimeters. Crop evapotranspiration can also be derived from meteorological and crop data by means of the FAO-PM ETo equation (Equation 2.1). By adjusting the albedo and the aerodynamic and canopy surface resistances to the growing characteristics of the specific crop, the evapotranspiration rate can be directly estimated using the Penman-Monteith combination equation (Equation 2.3). The albedo and resistances are, however, difficult to estimate accurately as they may vary continually during the growing season as climatic conditions change, as the crop develops, and with the wetness of the soil surface. The canopy resistance will further be influenced by the soil water availability, and it increases strongly if the crop is subjected to water stress. As there is still a considerable lack of consolidated information on the aerodynamic and canopy resistances for the various cropped surfaces, the FAO-PM ETo equation is used in these guidelines only for estimatin

In the crop coefficient approach the crop evapotranspiration, ETc, is calculated by multiplying the reference crop evapotranspiration, ETo, by a crop coefficient, Kc: where ETc crop evapotranspiration [mm d-1] ETo reference crop evapotranspiration [mm d-1] Most of the effects of the various weather conditions are incorporated into the ETo estimate. Therefore, as ETo represents an index of climatic demand, Kc varies predominately with the specific crop characteristics and only to a limited extent with climate. This enables the transfer of standard values for Kc between locations and between climates. This has been a primary reason for the global acceptance and usefulness of the crop coefficient approach and the Kc standard values developed in past studies. The reference ETo is defined and calculated using the FAO-PM ETo equation (Chapters 2 and 4). The

chapter: Chapter 5 — Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and its measurement

text: and usefulness of the crop coefficient approach and the Kc standard values developed in past studies. The reference ETo is defined and calculated using the FAO-PM ETo equation (Chapters 2 and 4). The crop coefficient, Kc, is basically the ratio of the crop ETc to the reference ETo, and it represents an integration of the effects of four primary characteristics that distinguish the crop from the reference grass. These characteristics are: • Crop height: the crop height influences the aerodynamic resistance term, ra, of the FAO-PM ETo equation and the turbulent transfer of vapour from the crop into the atmosphere. The ra term appears twice in the full form of the FAO-PM ETo • Albedo (reflectance) of the crop-soil surface: the albedo is affected by the fraction of ground covered by vegetation and by the soil surface wetness. The albedo of the crop-soil surface influences the net radiation of the surface, Rn, which is the primary source of the energy exchange for the evaporation process. • Canopy resistance: the resistance of the crop to vapour transfer is affected by leaf area (number of stomata), leaf age and condition, and the degree of stomatal control. The canopy resistance influ

text: • Canopy resistance: the resistance of the crop to vapour transfer is affected by leaf area (number of stomata), leaf age and condition, and the degree of stomatal control. The canopy resistance influences the surface resistance, rs. • Evaporation from soil, especially exposed soil. The soil surface wetness and the fraction of ground covered by vegetation influence the surface resistance, rs. Following soil wetting, the vapour transfer rate from the soil is high, especially for crops having incomplete ground cover. The combined surface resistance of the canopy and the soil determines the (bulk) surface resistance, rs. The surface resistance term in the Penman-Monteith combination Equation 2.3 represents the resistance to vapour flow from within plant leaves and from beneath the soil surface. The Kc in Equation 5.1 predicts ETc under standard conditions. The standard condition represents an upper envelope of crop evapotranspiration and represents conditions where no limitations are placed on crop growth or evapotranspiration due to water shortage, low crop density, or disease, weed, insect, or salinity pressures. The ETc estimated by Kc is adjusted if necessary to non-standard condi

text: The crop coefficient integrates the effect of characteristics that distinguish a typical field crop from the grass reference, where the standardized grass reference has a constant appearance and a complete ground cover. Consequently, different crops will have different Kc coefficients. The changing characteristics of the crop over the growing season affect the Kc coefficient. Finally, as evaporation is an integrated part of crop evapotranspiration, conditions affecting soil evaporation will also have an effect on Kc. Due to differences in albedo, crop height, aerodynamic properties, and leaf and stomata properties, the evapotranspiration from full-grown, well-watered crops differs from ETo. The close spacings of plants and taller canopy height and roughness of many full- grown agricultural crops cause these crops to have Kc factors that are larger than 1. The Kc factor is often 5-10 percent higher than the reference (where Kc = 1.0), and even 15-20 percent greater for some tall crops such as maize, sorghum or sugar cane (Figure 5.1). Species with stomata on only the lower side of the leaf and/or large leaf resistances will have relatively smaller Kc values. This is the case for citrus and most deciduous fruit trees. Because aerodynamic properties are greater for many agricultural crops as compared to the grass reference, the ratio of ETc to ETo (i.e. Kc) for many crops increases as wind speed increases and as relative humidity decreases. More arid climates and conditions of greater wind speed will tend to have higher values for Kc. More humid climates and conditions of lower wind speed will have lower values for Kc. This is because full-cover agricultural crops and the reference crop of clipped grass both provide for nearly maximum absorption of shortwave radiation, which is the primary energy source for evaporation under humid and calm conditions. Generally, the albedos, α, are similar over a wide range of full-cover agricultural crops, including the reference crop. Because the vapour pressure deficit (es − ea) is small under humid conditions, differences in ET caused by differences in aerodynamic resistance, ra, between the agricultural crop and the reference crop are also small, especially with low to moderate wind speed. Under arid conditions, the effect of differences in ra between the agricultural crop and the grass reference crop on ETc becomes more pronounced because the (es − ea) term may be relatively large. The larger magnitudes of (es − ea) amplify differences in the aerodynamic term in the numerator of the Penman-Monteith combination equation (Equation 2.1) for both the crop and the reference crop. Hence, Kc will be larger under arid conditions when the agricultural crop has a leaf area and roughness height that are greater than that of the grass reference. Because the 1/ra term in the numerator of the FAO-PM ETo equation (Equation 2.4 and 2.5a, b) is multiplied by the vapour pressure deficit (es − ea), the ET from tall crops increases proportionately more relative to ETo than does ET from short crops when relative humidity is low. The Kc for tall crops, such as those 2-3 m in height, can be as much as 30 percent higher in a windy, arid climate as compared with a calm, humid climate. The increase in Kc is due to the influence of the larger aerodynamic roughness of the tall crop relative to grass on the transport of water vapour from the surface. Differences in soil evaporation and crop transpiration between field crops and the reference surface are integrated within the crop coefficient. The Kc coefficient for full- cover crops primarily reflects differences in transpiration as the contribution of soil evaporation is relatively small. After rainfall or irrigation, the effect of evaporation is predominant when the crop is small and scarcely shades the ground. For such low- cover conditions, the Kc coefficient is determined largely by the frequency with which the soil surface is wetted. Where the soil is wet for most of the time from irrigation or rain, the evaporation from the soil surface will be considerable and Kc may exceed 1. On the other hand, where the soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted, and Kc will be small and might even drop to less than 0.20 (Figure 5.3). The length of the initial period is highly dependent on the crop, the crop variety, 5. Introduction to crop evapotranspiration (ETc ) and its measurement 143 the planting date, and the climate. The end of the initial period is determined as the time when approximately 10 percent of the ground surface is covered by green vegetation. For perennial crops, the planting date is replaced by the “greenup” date, i.e. the time when the initiation of new leaves occurs, or in other cases by the “sprouting” date, i.e. the time when the dormancy phase of the sprout buds ends. During the initial period, the leaf area is small, and evapotranspiration is predominantly in the form of soil evaporation. Therefore, the Kc during the initial period (Kc ini) is large when the soil is wet from irrigation and rainfall and is low when the soil surface is dry (Figure 5.5). Because it is difficult to visually determine when densely sown vegetation such as winter and spring cereals and some grasses reach effective full cover, the more easily detectable stage of heading (flowering) is generally used for these types of crops. For dense grasses, effective full cover may occur at about 0.10-0.15 m in height. For thin stands of grass (dry rangeland), grass height may approach 0.3-0.5 m before effective full cover is reached. Densely planted forages such as alfalfa and clover reach effective full cover at about 0.3-0.4 m. Another way to estimate the occurrence of effective full cover is when the leaf area index (LAI) reaches three in case of very dense low crops. As the crop develops and shades more and more of the ground, evaporation becomes more restricted, and transpiration gradually becomes the major process. During the crop development stage, the Kc value corresponds to the amounts of ground cover and plant development. Typically, if the soil surface is dry, Kc = 0.5 corresponds to about 25-40 percent of the ground surface covered by vegetation due to the effects of shading and due to microscale transport of sensible heat from the soil into the vegetation. The mid-season stage runs from effective full cover to the start of maturity. The start of maturity is often indicated by the beginning of the aging, yellowing or senescence of leaves, initial leaf drop, or the browning of fruit to the degree that the crop evapotranspiration is reduced relative to the reference ETo. The mid-season stage is the longest stage for perennials and many annuals, but it may be relatively short for vegetable crops that are harvested fresh for their green vegetation. At the mid-season stage the Kc reaches its maximum value. The value for Kc (Kc mid) is relatively constant for most growing and cultural conditions, namely for both evergreen and deciduous woody perennials. The Kcb represents the baseline standard Kc in the absence of the additional effects of soil wetting by irrigation or precipitation. The basal crop coefficient, Kcb, can also be defined as the ratio of transpiration, Tc to ETo. Therefore, it is also called the transpiration coefficient. The soil evaporation coefficient, Ke, describes the evaporation component from the soil surface. If the soil is wet, following rain or irrigation, Ke may be large. However, the sum of Kcb and Ke can never exceed a maximum value, Kc max, determined by the energy available for evapotranspiration at the soil surface. text: The main methods for measuring actual and standard ETc are described in the last section of Chapter 1, namely the soil water balance in lysimeters or the field, and the surface energy balance performed with ground and remote sensing approaches. That section is intended to draw the readers' attention to the need for accuracy in the determination of crop ET, thus discussing some critical aspects that affect measurement accuracy and the main pitfalls to be avoided. Over the last 25 years, hundreds of scientific papers have been published reporting crop ET measurements or estimates, and new (updated) Kc and Kcb values for nearly all vegetable and field crops, as well as for fruit trees and vines. As a follow-up, the current section presents several examples of procedures for determining crop coefficients using ground and remote sensing techniques. The evaporation coefficient, Ke, was calculated using the FAO56 procedure and the transpiration component, Kcb, was estimated from lysimeter Kc minus calculated Ke Note: Both different standard values for both years were obtained from adjustments to climate Determination of Kc using spectral reflectance from remote sensing Actual Kcb and Kc values can be estimated using remote sensing based on field, aerial or satellite platforms, using empirical approaches based on spectral reflectance. Remote observations of Kcb and Kc are valuable when field information, such as planting dates or rates of vegetation development, are not well known. The estimation of Kcb from reflectance-based vegetation indices (VI) is possible because of the generally close correspondence between vegetation amount and transpiration, where, as vegetation cover increases, leaf area increases and transpiration and Kcb increase. The crop coefficients obtained from reflectance represent the actual ET conditions of the field (ideal or nonideal) and are termed Kcb act RS and Kc act RS. text: coefficients obtained from reflectance represent the actual ET conditions of the field (ideal or nonideal) and are termed Kcb act RS and Kc act RS. Challenges with VI-based estimation of the single Kc, that includes the evaporation component, is that spectral-reflectance-based observations generally cannot detect the presence of wet soil. Therefore, independent methods that use knowledge of specific wetting events are needed for estimating the evaporation from bare soil following precipitation and irrigation events. Wetting information is often difficult to obtain for specific fields, so that an empirically-based adjustment or coefficient is required to convert remotely-based Kcb into an equivalent Kc. Remotely-sensed Kcb act RS and Kc act RS may also have difficulty in capturing the reduced ET associated with water stress caused by short-term soil-water shortage because the short-term water stress is generally not indicated by a significant change in VI. Under water shortage, a thermally-based method described in the next section may be required. text: Determination of Kc using energy balance from remote sensing The remote sensing surface energy balance (RS-SEB) method was introduced and described in Chapter 1. Over the last 25 years, various remote sensing approaches based on surface energy balance have been developed and widely used. RS-SEB methods take advantage of the physical fact that conversion of liquid water to vapour requires very substantial amounts of energy. This conversion of liquid to vapour during the evaporation process involves the same physical requirements whether the process is the transpiration of water from inside a plant leaf or the evaporation of water from a wet soil surface. The energy consumption by the conversion of liquid to vapour cools the evaporating surface, thus variations in surface temperature can be used to estimate the net radiation and sensible heat exchange at the surface. These estimates can then be used with the energy balance equation (Equation 1.1) to estimate the crop evapotranspiration. Determinations of reduced ET from water stress can be made difficult, however, by uncertainties, inaccuracies and biases in both modeling approaches. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for developing Kc data Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms can ingest data from remote sensing, weather stations, and ground measurements to learn complex relationships observed among different factors and ET rates. AI models can help reduce uncertainty in ET estimations by learning from various data sources and accounting for land cover dynamics. This can lead to better water management practices and a more comprehensive understanding of the water cycle. However, AI can not directly recognize nor correct for faulty data that is ingested into the process.  This is most true with Kc data, where substantial errors and biases in both ground-based and remote-sensing-based measurements can frequently occur. The application of powerful cognition and ingestion of large amounts of data does not o

The application of powerful cognition and ingestion of large amounts of data does not offset nor cure the impacts of faulty, biased data. In fact, AI may magnify the influences of biased or faulty ET data on derived relationships. The result can be a worse estimation of ET as compared to using direct Kc curves or remotely-sensed ET procedures alone. Therefore, strong precautions should be taken, along with a required precursor involving a study of the physics of the evapotranspiration processes, impacts of agronomic practices and plant physiology. Some advantages of employing AI can include the classification of crop type in near real time. Near-real-time classification, for example using satellite imagery, can facilitate the forecasting of near- and mid-term, field-specific ET for irrigation management. Given accurate Kc estimation from remote sensing models, AI can help to analyze and develop ranges of Kc within populations of the same crop type. AI can also be employed to develop or expand the use of growing degree days for estimating Kc curve development. However, an

text: ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) This chapter deals with the calculation of crop evapotranspiration (ETc) under standard, pristine, non-stressed cropping conditions. No limitations are placed on crop growth and evapotranspiration from soil water and salinity stress, reduced crop density, pests and diseases, weed infestation, or low fertility and nutrients (see Figure 1.4 bis). ETc is determined by the crop coefficient approach whereby the effect of the various weather conditions are incorporated into ETo and the crop characteristics into The single Kc coefficient incorporates crop characteristics and averaged effects of evaporation from the soil. For normal irrigation planning and management purposes, for the development of basic irrigation schedules, and for most hydrologic water balance studies, average crop coefficients are relevant and may be more convenient than the Kc computed on a daily time step using the dual Kc approach where a separate crop transpiration and soil evaporation coefficient are determined (Chapter 7). Only when values for Kc are needed on a daily basis for specific fields of crops and/or for specific years, or where wetting frequencies from precipitatio

chapter: Chapter 6 — ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc)
locator: Chapter 6 — ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc)
text: ation coefficient are determined (Chapter 7). Only when values for Kc are needed on a daily basis for specific fields of crops and/or for specific years, or where wetting frequencies from precipitation or irrigation are frequent or varied, must a separate transpiration and evaporation coefficient (Kcb + Ke) be considered. The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ETc, consists of: 1. identifying the crop growth stages, selecting the corresponding Kc coefficients and determining their stage lengths; 2. adjusting the selected Kc coefficients for frequency of wetting or climatic 3. constructing the crop coefficient curve, i.e. providing to determine Kc values for any period during the growing season; and 4. calculating ETc as the product of ETo and Kc. Changes in vegetation and ground cover imply that the crop coefficient Kc varies during the growing season. The trends in Kc during the growing season are represented in the crop coefficient segmented curve. Only three values for Kc are required to describe and construct the crop coefficient curve: those during the initial stage (Kc ini), the mid-season stage (Kc mid) and at the end of the late season stage (Kc end). text: Reference evapotranspiration (ETo), standard crop evapotranspiration (ETc) and The tabulated standard coefficients are single values that integrate the effects of both transpiration and evaporation over time. The effects of the integration over time represent an average wetting frequency for a “standard” crop under typical growing conditions in an irrigated setting. The vegetable crops and the orchard and vineyard crops generally represent evaporation associated with drip irrigation, thus having frequent applications of small irrigation depths, while field crops and grasses, when irrigated, are mostly considered to be under surface or sprinkler irrigation. Naturally, wetlands and riparian vegetation are not irrigated. The values for Kc (Tables 6.1 through 6.5) during the initial and crop development stages can be subject to the effects of large variations in wetting frequencies by rainfall (and irrigation) and, therefore, refinements to the value used for Kc ini should always be made with consideration of the impacts of rainfall and/or irrigation on soil evaporation, especially when the presence of bare soil can dominate. Kc values are assigned to groups of somewhat similar grass crops, but alfalfa is individually considered. Grasslands are kept low if used for grazing and landscape, or with a variable height during every cutting cycle. Their Kc values were not adjusted to climate. Users should compare the local climate with the standardized climate (RHmin of about 45 percent and with calm to moderate wind speeds averaging u2 = 2 m s-1) and adjust Kc values when required. Moreover, the Kc values should be reduced by 10 to 30 percent when vegetation conditions or cultivation practices are not optimal and depart from the standard. Considering the worldwide need for water saving, the Kc values for irrigated crops in Tables 6.1 through 6.4 are the maximal values to be adopted when computing ETc for irrigation scheduling. For water savings in irrigation, these tabulated Kc mid values can be decreased by 10 to 30 percent to correspond with soil water depletion thresholds associated with moderating yield losses resulting from water stress

Grasses for hay, grazing and landscape Wetlands are among the main protected vegetation and ecosystems, and their management requires estimation of evapotranspiration and water availability for their vegetation and for external use. Wetlands consist of areas where water covers the soil or is present either at near the soil surface all year or for varying periods of time during the year, namely during part of the growing season. Water saturation of the soils, together with climate, largely determines the soil evolution and hydric soil characteristics, and the types of plant and animal communities living in and on the soil. Wetlands may support both aquatic and terrestrial species. The continued presence of water favours conditions adequate for the growth of hydrophyte plants and characteristic ecosystems. The time interval between wetting events Evapotranspiration during the initial stage for annual crops is predominately in the form of evaporation from exposed soil due to low levels of vegetation. Therefore, accurate estimates for Kc ini should consider the frequency with which the soil surface is wetted during the initial period. Where the soil is frequently or continuously wet from irrigation, rain, or a natural surface or groundwater source, the evaporation from the soil surface can be considerable and Kc ini will be large, e.g. flooded rice and wetlands vegetation. On the other hand, where the soil surface is dry, evaporation is restricted and the Kc ini will be small (Table 5.1). The value for Kc ini is affected by the evaporating power of the atmosphere, i.e. which is indicated by ETo. The higher the evaporation power of the atmosphere, the quicker the soil will dry between water applications and the smaller the time- averaged Kc ini will be for any particular period. ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) 179 Time interval between wetting events under irrigation For estimating Kc ini, a mean time interval between wetting events is estimated by counting all rainfall and irrigation events occurring during the initial period that are greater than a few millimetres. Wetting events occurring on adjacent days can be counted as one event. The mean wetting interval is estimated by dividing the time length (days) of the initial period by the number of events (Example 6.1).

text: Kc ini for flooded rice and wetlands for various climatic conditions Background and computations for Kc for the initial stage Evaporation from bare soil (Es) can be characterized as occurring in two distinct stages. Stage 1 is termed the "energy-limited" stage. During this stage, moisture is transported to the soil surface at a rate sufficient to supply the potential rate of evaporation (Eso), which, in turn, is governed by energy availability at the soil surface. In this procedure, where Eso is the potential rate of evaporation [mm d-1] and ETo is the mean ETo during the initial period [mm d-1]. The value 1.15 represents increased evaporation potential due to the low albedo of wet soil and the possibility of heat stored in the surface layer Stage 2 is termed the "soil water limited" stage, where hydraulic transport of subsurface water to the soil surface is unable to supply water at the potential evaporation rate. During stage 2, the soil surface appears partially dry and a portion of the evaporation occurs from below the soil surface. The energy required for subsurface evaporation is supplied by the transport of heat from the soil surface into the soil profile. The evaporation ra

The evaporation rate during stage 2 drying decreases as soil water content decreases as shown in Figure 6.4. The evaporation rate can therefore be expressed as being proportional to the water remaining in the evaporation layer relative to the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated from the same soil layer during stage 2 drying. The background of this procedure is the same as for the computation of the evaporation coefficient Ke in the dual crop coefficient approach dealt with in Chapter 7, where further details are provided. The maximum total depth of water that can be evaporated from the surface soil layer is termed “total evaporable water” or TEW. In turn, the maximum total depth of water that can be evaporated during stage 1 is termed “readily evaporable water” or REW, which is discussed in Chapter 7. text: THE LATE SEASON STAGE (Kc end) Typical values for the crop coefficient at the end of the late season stage, Kc end, are listed in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 for various agricultural crops and land covers. The values given for Kc end reflect crop and water management practices particular to those crops and vegetation. If the crop is irrigated frequently until harvested fresh, the topsoil remains wet and the Kc end value will be relatively high. On the other hand, crops that are allowed to senesce and dry out in the field before harvest receive less frequent irrigation or no irrigation at all during the late season stage. Consequently, both the soil surface and vegetation are dry and the value for Kc end will be relatively small (Figure 6.6). Where the local water management and harvest timing practices are known to deviate from the typical ones, the user should make adequate adjustments to the values for Kc end. Some guidance on the adjustment of Kc values for wetting frequency is provided in Chapter 7. For premature harvest, the user can construct a Kc curve using the Kc end value provided in Tables 6.1 – 6.5 and a late season length typical of a normal harvest date; and then the user should

text: 6. ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) 197 Many crops grown for forage or hay are harvested/cut several times during the growing season. Each cut essentially terminates a “sub” growing cycle and an associated Kc curve, and initiates a new “sub” growing cycle and associated Kc curve. The resulting Kc curve for the entire growing season is the aggregation of a series of Kc curves associated with each sub-cycle. Figure 6.8 presents a Kc curve for the entire growing season constructed for alfalfa grown for hay in southern Idaho, USA. A larger number of cuts may be considered for other locations depending on forage species, management of the forage or grassland and on climate (see Table 6.4).

chapter: Chapter 6 — ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc)
locator: Chapter 6 — ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) — Alfalfa-Based Crop Coefficients
text: As two reference crop definitions (grass and alfalfa) are in use in various parts of the world, two families of Kc curves for agricultural crops have been developed in the literature. These are the alfalfa-based Kc curves and the grass-based curves in FAO 24 and in the original version of the current FAO 56, and those reported herein. The user must exercise caution to avoid mixing grass-based Kc values with alfalfa reference ET and vice versa. Usually, a Kc based on the alfalfa reference can be “converted” for use with a grass reference by multiplying by a factor ranging from about 1.05 to 1.35, depending on the climate (1.05 for humid, calm conditions, and 1.2 for semi-arid, moderately windy conditions, and 1.35 for arid, windy conditions): A reference conversion ratio can be established for any climate by using the Kc mid = 1.20 listed for alfalfa in Table 6.4 and then adjusting this Kc mid for the climate using Equation 6.16. For example, at Kimberly, Idaho, the United States, where RHmin = 30 percent and u2 = 2.2 m s-1 are average values during the summer months, a reference conversion ratio between alfalfa and grass references using Equation 6.16 is approximately: where h = 0.

text: Thermal lengths of the crop growth stages The construction of the crop coefficient curve requires the estimation of the lengths of the four stages that connect or represent the three Kc values. These stages are the initial (ini), development (dev), mid-season (mid) and late-season (end) as in Figure 6.7 and In the absence of limiting factors such as water or nutrients, a crop’s development essentially depends on the temperature accumulation over time. Thus, the use of thermal time or growing degree days (GDD) to estimate the crop growth stage lengths has the merits of allowing one to adequately extrapolate from one year to the next, to diverse locations, and to take into consideration the impacts of climate change, particularly in temperature, on crop growth cycles. The use of GDD is important for studies relating to the assessment of climate change impacts on water and irrigation requirements. Therefore, in this updated publication, the use of GDD to determine the lengths of crop growth stages and the shape of the seasonal Kc curve is provided rather than static stage lengths as provided in the 1998 FAO56 publication. Stage lengths, expressed in days, are available in the previous

ETc and single crop coefficients (Kc) 203 The time of emergence of vegetation and the time of effective full cover can be estimated using sophisticated plant growth models or by cumulative GDD regression equations. While those models should be verified or validated for the local area or for a specific crop variety using local observations, the use of generalized GDD is a more simplified but reliable method that can be applied using simple computer software or spreadsheets. Crop growth and development of the Kc curve is assumed to occur on any day when the mean air temperature exceeds a lower temperature threshold termed the base temperature (Tbase). The value of Tbase depends on the crop and variety. In conjunction with Tbase , when the mean daily air temperature exceeds an upper temperature threshold (Tupper), crop development is assumed to be limited to the GDD below that limit. Therefore, the length of time between planting and effective full cover will vary with climate, latitude, elevation, and planting date. It will also vary with cultivar (crop variety). Generally, once the effective full cover for a plant canopy has been reached, the rate of further phenological development (flowering, fruit development, ripening, and senescence) is more dependent on plant genotype and less dependent on weather. chapter: Chapter 7 — ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke)
locator: Chapter 7 — ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke)
text: ETc and dual crop coefficient This chapter, complementing Chapter 6, deals with the calculation of crop evapotranspiration (ETc) under standard, non-stressed cropping conditions where no limitations are placed on crop growth or evapotranspiration. This chapter presents the procedure for predicting the effects of specific wetting events on the value of the crop coefficient Kc. The solution consists of splitting Kc into two separate coefficients, one for crop transpiration, i.e. the basal crop coefficient (Kcb), and one for soil evaporation (Ke): The dual crop coefficient approach is more complicated and more computationally intensive than the single crop coefficient approach (Kc) dealt with in Chapter 6. The procedure is conducted on a daily basis and is intended for applications using computers. It is recommended that the approach be followed when improved estimates for Kc are needed, for example, to schedule irrigations for individual fields on a daily basis, mainly in case of incomplete cover crops, or to increase accuracy in hydrologic studies. The calculation procedure for crop evapotranspiration, ETc, consists of: 1. identifying the lengths of crop growth stages, and selecting

locator: Chapter 7 — ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) — Transpiration Component (Kcb Eto)
text: The basal crop coefficient (Kcb) is defined as the ratio of the crop evapotranspiration over the grass reference evapotranspiration (ETc/ETo) when the soil surface is dry but transpiration is occurring at a potential rate, i.e. water is not limiting transpiration (Figure 5.3). Therefore, “Kcb ETo” represents primarily the transpiration component of ETc and Kcb is often called transpiration coefficient. The Kcb ETo does include a small, residual diffusive evaporation component supplied by soil water below the dry surface and by soil water from beneath dense vegetation. As the Kc values of Chapter 6 include averaged effects of evaporation from the soil surface, the Kcb values lie below the Kc values as illustrated in Figure 5.7 and a separate table for Kcb is required. Recommended values for Kcb are listed in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 for the same crops listed in Tables 6.1 to 6.3. Values tabulated in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 do not include the influence of mulches, which are dealt with in Chapter 10. As with Tables 6.1 to 6.3, the values for Kcb in Tables 7.1 to 7.3 represent Kcb for a standardized sub-humid climate and with moderate wind speed. Where the topsoil is wet, following rain or irrigation, Ke is maximal. Where the soil surface is dry, Ke is small and even zero if no water remains near the soil surface for evaporation. Two calculation procedures are presented, the FAO56 original and the skin layer evaporation approach, which consists of a refinement of the former to increase accuracy, mainly for small wetting depths.

During stage 1 of the drying process, the soil surface remains wet and it is assumed that evaporation from soil exposed to the atmosphere will occur at the maximum rate limited only by energy availability at the soil surface. This stage holds until the cumulative depth of evaporation, De, is such that the hydraulic properties of the upper soil become limiting, and water cannot be transported to the soil surface at a rate that can supply the potential demand. During stage 1 drying, Kr = 1.0. The cumulative depth of evaporation, De, at the end of stage 1 drying is REW (readily evaporable water, which is the maximum depth of water that can be evaporated from the topsoil layer without restriction during stage 1). locator: Chapter 7 — ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) — The Skin Layer Approach
text: The use of the fraction of the time step calculation (day or hour) that resides in stage 1 evaporation, Astage 1, is an extension to the original FAO 56 approach to provide more precise definition of the transition from stage 1 to stage 2 drying during a time step. The improved definition can be important when using daily calculation time steps, especially for coarse soils having small REW. The skin layer approach improves daily estimates for Ke when the depths of wetting events are small. Small depths of wetting occur when precipitation or sprinkler irrigation events are less than about 10 mm. If small wetting events occur when the total 100 to 150 mm deep soil evaporation layer is dry (De,i ~ TEW), then much of the added water remains close to the top of the soil evaporation layer and tends to evaporate quickly. The original procedure implicitly assumes that small water additions are mixed throughout the soil evaporation layer. As a result, the original procedure tends to extend the evaporation of the added water over a number of days at a relatively low rate due to small values calculated for Kr. In contrast, the skin evaporation extension retains water close to the surface in t

chapter: Chapter 7 — ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke)
locator: Chapter 7 — ETc and dual crop coefficient (Kc = Kcb + Ke) — The Skin Layer Approach
text: evaporation of the added water over a number of days at a relatively low rate due to small values calculated for Kr. In contrast, the skin evaporation extension retains water close to the surface in the REW zone, so the Es rate is generally higher in value and shorter in time. The skin evaporation extension tends to reproduce the relatively short-lived and higher magnitude Stage 1 spikes of Es and Ke that are observed in field monitoring. It is important to note that the skin evaporation extension and the original Ke computation procedure will generally produce similar total depths of evaporation over an extended period. This is because both methods adhere to a water balance of the topsoil and to the conservation of mass. The difference is in the duration and magnitude of Ke. These differences in daily estimates may not matter when estimating total water consumption (ET) over extended periods. The skin evaporation extension may be most important when comparing ET estimates to ground or remote sensing observations where the timing and magnitude of evaporation on a specific day is important. The skin evaporation extension can be applied to daily or hourly calculation timesteps. As fo

The advantage of the calculation of Astage 1 and DREW is that small irrigation or precipitation events may only wet the REW (“skin”) of the soil, but not the entire Ze depth of the evaporation layer. The inclusion of Astage 1 and DREW will cause the estimate for Ke to “spike” towards 1.0 following a light wetting event for a short period of time. This is quite common where light wetting events wet only the upper skin of soil and evaporate off relatively quickly. Those events may be less effective in replenishing the root zone. The calculation of De,i and DREW,i requires that first Kr is calculated from Equation 7.11. Therefore, the calculation of Kr is based on the ending depletion of the previous day or time period, i-1. Daily precipitation in amounts less than about 0.2 ETo is normally entirely evaporated and can usually be ignored in the Ke and water balance calculations. However, small amounts of precipitation are also correctly dealt with by Equation 7.11 – 7.15. Light precipitation events will generally have little or no runoff. The amount of rainfall lost by runoff depends on: the intensity of rainfall; the slope of land; the soil type, its hydraulic conditions and antecedent moisture content; and the land use and cover. For general situations where many irrigated fields have small slopes, ROi can be assumed to be zero or can be accounted for by considering only a certain percentage of Pi. text: ETc under soil water and salinity Forces acting on the soil water decrease its potential energy and make it less available for plant root extraction. When the soil is wet, the water has a high potential energy, is relatively free to move and is easily taken up by the plant roots. In dry soils, the water has a low potential energy and is strongly bound by capillary and absorptive forces to the soil matrix and is less easily extracted by the crop. When the potential energy of the soil water drops below a threshold value, the crop is said to be water stressed. The effects of soil water stress are described by multiplying the basal crop coefficient by the water stress coefficient, Ks: For soil water limiting conditions, Ks < 1. Where there is no soil water deficit, Ks = 1. Ks describes the effect of water stress on crop transpiration. Where the single crop coefficient is used, the effect of water stress is incorporated into Kc as: ETc  act = Ks Kc ETo = Kc  act ETo (8.2) Salinity also decreases the potential energy of the soil water and makes water more difficult to be extracted by the plant roots. Thus Equations 8.1 and 8.2 also apply when salinity of the soil and the irrigation water

text: eases the potential energy of the soil water and makes water more difficult to be extracted by the plant roots. Thus Equations 8.1 and 8.2 also apply when salinity of the soil and the irrigation water affect extraction by the roots, with Ks becoming a salinity and water stress coefficient, i.e. salinity and water stress combine in Ks < 1 as developed later in this chapter. Because the water stress coefficient impacts only crop transpiration, rather than evaporation from soil, the application of Ks using Equation 8.1 is generally more accurate than its application using Equation 8.2. However, in situations where evaporation from soil is not a large component of ETc, the use of Equation 8.2 will provide quite reasonable results.

locator: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions — Soil Water Availability
text: Soil water availability refers to the capacity of a soil to retain water available to plants. After heavy rainfall or irrigation, the soil will drain until field capacity is reached. Field capacity is the amount of water that a well-drained soil should hold against gravitational forces, or the amount of water remaining when downward drainage has markedly decreased. In the absence of water supply, the water content in the root zone decreases as a result of water uptake by the crop. As water uptake progresses, the remaining water is held to the soil particles with greater force, lowering its potential energy and making it more difficult for the plant to extract it. Eventually, a point is reached where the crop can no longer extract the remaining water. The water uptake becomes zero when wilting point is reached. Wilting point is the water content at which plants will permanently wilt. As the water content above field capacity cannot be held against the forces of gravity and will drain, and as the water content below wilting point cannot be extracted by plant roots, the total available water in the root zone is the difference between the water content at field capacity and wilting poi

The rate of root water uptake is, in fact, influenced more directly by the potential energy level of the soil water (soil matric potential and the associated hydraulic conductivity) than by water content alone. As a certain soil matric potential corresponds in different soil types with different soil water contents, the value for p is also a function of the soil type. However, values for MAD are influenced by management and economic factors in addition to the physical factors influencing p. Generally, MAD < RAW where there is risk aversion or uncertainty, and MAD > RAW where plant moisture deficit is an intentional part of soil water management.

text: The estimation of Ks requires a daily water balance computation for the root zone. Schematically (Figure 8.4), the root zone can be presented by means of a container in which the water content may fluctuate. To express the water content as root zone depletion is useful. It makes the adding and subtracting of losses and gains straightforward as the various parameters of the soil water budget are usually expressed in terms of water depth. Rainfall, irrigation, and capillary rise of groundwater towards the root zone add water to the root zone and decrease the root zone depletion. Soil evaporation, crop transpiration and percolation losses remove water from the root zone and increase the depletion. text: Water balance of the soil root zone In Figure 8.4 it is assumed that water can be stored in the root zone until field capacity is reached. Although following heavy rain or irrigation the water content might temporally exceed field capacity, the total amount of water above field capacity is assumed to be lost the same day by deep percolation, following any ET for that day. By assuming that the root zone is at field capacity following heavy rain or irrigation, the minimum value for the depletion Dr,i is zero. As a result of percolation and evapotranspiration, the water content in the root zone will gradually decrease and the root zone depletion will increase. In the absence of any wetting event, the water content will steadily reach its minimum value θWP. At that moment no water is left for evapotranspiration in the root zone, Ks becomes zero, and the root zone depletion has reached its maximum value TAW. chapter: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions
locator: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions — Forecasting Or Allocating Irrigations
text: Irrigation is required when rainfall is insufficient to compensate for the soil water used as evapotranspiration. The primary objective of irrigation is to apply water at the right time and in the right amount. The timing and depth of future irrigations can be planned by calculating the soil water balance of the root zone on a daily basis (Equation 8.7). To avoid crop water stress, irrigations should be applied before or at the moment when the readily available soil water is depleted so that Dr,i is always ≤ RAW. To avoid deep percolation losses that may leach valuable nutrients out of the root zone, the net irrigation depth should be smaller than or equal to the root zone depletion (Ii ≤ Dr,i) unless leaching of salts is needed. Example 8.3 illustrates the application of a water balance of the root zone to predict irrigation dates to avoid water stress. The example utilizes various calculations for Ke Boxes 8.3 and 8.4 show, respectively, an application of the dual Kc approach to a water- stressed soybean crop and to a hedgerow olive orchard under deficit irrigation management.

chapter: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions
locator: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions — Stress Effects Of Soil Salinity
text: Salts in the soil water solution can reduce evapotranspiration by making soil water less "available" for plant root extraction. Salts have an affinity for water and hence additional force is required for the crop to extract water from a saline soil. The presence of salts in the soil water solution reduces the total potential energy of the soil water solution. In addition, some salts may cause toxic effects in plants and can reduce plant metabolism, growth and yield. A function is presented hereafter that predicts the reduction in evapotranspiration caused by the salinity of soil water. The function is derived by combining yield-salinity equations from the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No29 with yield-ET equations from FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No33. The resulting equation provides a first approximation to the reduction in evapotranspiration expected under various salinity conditions. Salinity impacts and crops tolerance There is evidence that crop yield and transpiration are not as sensitive to low osmotic potential as they are to low matric potential. Under saline conditions, many plants are able to partially compensate for the low osmotic potential of the soil water b

chapter: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions
locator: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions — Stress Effects Of Soil Salinity
text: e not as sensitive to low osmotic potential as they are to low matric potential. Under saline conditions, many plants are able to partially compensate for the low osmotic potential of the soil water by building up higher internal solute contents. This is done by absorbing ions from the soil solution and by synthesizing organic osmolytes. Both of these reactions reduce the impact of osmotic potential on water availability. However, the synthesis of organic osmolytes does require the expenditure of metabolic energy. Therefore, plant growth is often reduced under saline conditions. The reduced plant growth impacts transpiration by reducing ground cover, and a further reduction in transpiration is sometimes additionally caused by partial stomatal closure. Other impacts of salts in the soil include direct sodium and chloride toxicities and induced nutrient deficiencies. These deficiencies reduce plant growth by reducing the rate of leaf elongation, the enlargement, and the division of cells in leaves. The modality depends on the method of irrigation. With sprinkler irrigation, adsorption of sodium and chloride through the leaf can result in toxic conditions for all crop species. With su

chapter: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions

text: in leaves. The modality depends on the method of irrigation. With sprinkler irrigation, adsorption of sodium and chloride through the leaf can result in toxic conditions for all crop species. With surface or trickle irrigation, direct toxic conditions generally occur only in vine and tree crops; however, high levels of sodium can induce calcium deficiencies for all crop species. Since salt concentration changes as the soil water content changes, soil salinity is normally measured and expressed on the basis of the electrical conductivity of the saturation extract of the soil (ECe). The ECe is defined as the electrical conductivity of the soil water solution after the addition of a sufficient quantity of distilled water to bring the soil water content to saturation. ECe is typically expressed in deciSiemens per meter (dS m-1). Under optimum management conditions, crop yields remain at potential levels until a specific, threshold electrical conductivity of the saturation soil water extract (ECe threshold) is reached. If the average ECe of the root zone increases above this critical threshold value, the yield is presumed to begin to decrease linearly in proportion to the increase in s

locator: Chapter 8 — ETc under soil water and salinity stress conditions — Stress Effects Of Soil Salinity
text: ct (ECe threshold) is reached. If the average ECe of the root zone increases above this critical threshold value, the yield is presumed to begin to decrease linearly in proportion to the increase in salinity. The rate of decrease in yield with increase in salinity is usually expressed as a slope, b, having units of % reduction in yield per dS m-1 increase in ECe. All plants do not respond to salinity in a similar manner; some crops can produce acceptable yields at much higher soil salinity levels than others. This is because some crops are better able to make the needed osmotic adjustments that enable them to extract more water from a saline soil, or they may be more tolerant of some of the toxic effects of salinity. Salt tolerance for many agricultural crops is provided in the FAO Irrigation and Drainage Papers No. 33 and 48. The ECe, threshold and slope b from these and other sources are listed in Tables 8.8 through 8.11, respectively for vegetable, field, fruit tree and vine, and grass and forage crops. The data serve only as a guideline - tolerance vary depending on climate, soil conditions and cultural practices. Crops are often less tolerant during germination and seedling st

Crops are often less tolerant during germination and seedling stage. As can be observed from the data in these Tables, there is an 8 to 11-fold range in salt tolerance of agricultural crops. The effect of soil salinity on yield and crop evapotranspiration is hence crop specific. The ECe, threshold and b parameters in Tables 8.8 through 8.11 were determined primarily in research experiments using nearly steady-state irrigation where soil water contents were maintained at levels close to field capacity. However, under most types of irrigation scheduling for sprinkler and surface irrigation, the soil water content is typically depleted to well below field capacity, so that the EC of the soil water solution, ECsw, increases prior to irrigation, even though the EC of the saturation extract does not change. The increased salt concentration in the soil water solution reduces the osmotic potential of the soil water solution (it becomes more negative), so that the plant must expend more metabolic energy and may exert more mechanical force to absorb water. For many crops, the seasonal Ky is nearly 1.0 (Table 8.7). For crops where Ky is unknown, the user may assume Ky = 1 in Equations 8.19 and 8.25, or may select a Ky relative to a crop type that has similar behaviour. chapter: Chapter 9 — Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation
locator: Chapter 9 — Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation
text: Actual crop ET (ETc act) refers to both agricultural and natural vegetation including non- pristine agricultural vegetation. The latter is defined, in the usage here, as vegetation having less than perfect growing conditions or stand characteristics (i.e. relatively poor conditions of density, height, leaf area, fertility, vitality and biomass yield) as compared to “pristine” maximal yield conditions. Non-typical cropping conditions are also included and refer to types or arrangements of agricultural crops that are not listed or described in Tables 6.1 to 6.4 and 7.1 to 7.3. However, non-typical cropping conditions are mainly dealt with in Chapter 10. The approach whereby a crop is characterized by a crop coefficient, Kc, and the crop evapotranspiration is given by the product of Kc and the reference evapotranspiration ETo, provides a simple and convenient way of also characterizing the evapotranspiration from natural vegetation and for diverse non-typical cultivation practices. This chapter presents procedures for estimating actual Kc and Kcb values for natural vegetation and for agricultural vegetation independent of having Kc and Kcb values available. The section on estimating c

text: hapter presents procedures for estimating actual Kc and Kcb values for natural vegetation and for agricultural vegetation independent of having Kc and Kcb values available. The section on estimating crop coefficients from fraction of ground cover and crop height is particularly important because it focuses on the estimation of ETc act aimed at its use in irrigation scheduling and water management in real time.

chapter: Chapter 9 — Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation

text: The first step in the Kc ETo approach is the estimation of lengths of crop growth stages, which also applies to natural vegetation (Tables 6.4 and 6.5). The next step is the development of crop coefficient curves that represent the ratios of ETc to ETo during the various growth stages of the vegetation as described in Chapters 5 and 6. The procedure to estimate crop coefficients for the initial growth stage for agricultural non-pristine and natural vegetation is identical to that described for agricultural crops in Chapter 6 (single crop coefficient Kc ini) or Chapter 7 (dual crop coefficient, Kcb ini + Ke). The crop coefficient during this stage is primarily determined by the frequency with which the soil is wetted. Mid and late season stages The Kc act during the mid-season period (Kc mid act and Kcb mid act), and to a lesser extent the Kc act during the late season period, differ from those described in previous chapters 6 and 7. As the ground cover for non-pristine vegetation is often reduced, the Kc act is affected to a large extent by the frequency of precipitation and/or irrigation and by the amount of leaf area and ground cover. Natural vegetation, mainly when sparse, is af

Natural vegetation, mainly when sparse, is affected by the frequency of precipitation and the Kc act is dependent on the amount of leaf area and ground cover. The determination of Kc for non-pristine and natural vegetation should ordinarily follow the approach described in Chapter 7 whereby separate transpiration (Kcb) and evaporation (Ke) coefficients are used. chapter: Chapter 9 — Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation
locator: Chapter 9 — Actual crop ET (ETc act) by agricultural and natural vegetation — Cover And Height
text: A popular and generally successful method for estimating Kc is to base the estimate on the fraction of ground covered by vegetation and the height of the vegetation. These two parameters are the primary characteristics of vegetation that control the rate of ETc act in terms of its ratio to the grass reference ETo. This method, referred to as the Allen and Pereira (A&P) approach, is explained hereafter in Equations 9.8-9.14. For expanses of vegetation large enough that an equilibrium boundary layer is established, so that general one-dimensional equations such as the Penman-Monteith apply, a maximum upper limit on ET is established according to the law of conservation of energy. Thus, for expanses of vegetation larger than about 500 to 2 000 m2, the Kc will have upper limits of 1.2-1.3 for the grass reference. However, under conditions of "clothesline effects" (where vegetation height exceeds that of the surroundings) or "oasis effects" (where vegetation has higher soil water availability than the surroundings), peak Kc may attain larger values. chapter: Chapter 10 — ETc under various crop management practices
locator: Chapter 10 — ETc under various crop management practices
text: ETc act under various crop This chapter discusses various types of factors that may cause the values for Kc act and ETc act to deviate from the standard Kc and Kcb values described in Chapters 6 and 7. These factors refer to the effects of surface mulches, intercropping, small areas of vegetation and estimation of Kc or Kcb for periods under conditions of frozen soil as This chapter is intended to serve as a resource for situations where cultivation practices are known to deviate from those assumed in Tables 6.1 to 6.4 and 7.1 to 7.3 and where estimates of Kc act and ETc act are still necessary. This chapter is by no means exhaustive; its intent is to show some of the procedures that can be used to make adjustments to Kc to account for deviations from standard conditions.

chapter: Chapter 10 — ETc under various crop management practices
locator: Chapter 10 — ETc under various crop management practices — Effects Of Surface Mulches
text: Mulches are frequently used in vegetable production to reduce evaporation losses from the soil surface, to accelerate crop development in cool climates by increasing soil temperature, to reduce erosion, or to assist in weed control. Mulches may be composed of organic plant materials, or they may consist of plastic sheets or films. Plastic mulches generally consist of thin sheets of polyethylene, or a similar material placed over the ground surface, especially along the plant rows. Holes are cut into the plastic film at plant spacings to allow the plant vegetation to emerge. Plastic mulches can be transparent, white, or black. Colour influences albedo, mainly during the early stages of the crop. However, as the intention is to use a simple procedure for adjusting Kc for mulched crops, only generalized recommendations are given here. The published literature offers contradictory information on impacts of plastic mulches on Kc and ET. However, it appears likely that black plastic increases the soil temperature more than transparent plastic, so that transparent plastic may cause slightly smaller differences in Kc relative to not adopting any type of mulching. Plastic mulches can substantially reduce the evaporation of water from the soil surface. The impact of plastic mulch is likely more evident under trickle irrigation systems. Associated with the reduction in evaporation, however, there may occur a general increase in transpiration from the vegetation caused by the transfer of both sensible and radiative heat from the surface of the plastic cover to adjacent vegetation. Even though the transpiration rates under mulch may increase by an average of 10-30 percent over the season as compared to no mulch, the Kc values may decrease by an average of 10-30 percent due to a 30-80 percent reduction in soil evaporation. text: Intercropping refers to the situation where two different crops are grown together within one field. For the estimation of the crop coefficient, a distinction is made • contiguous vegetation, where the canopies of the two crops intermingle at some height (e.g. corn and beans intercropping); • overlapping crops, where the canopy of one crop is well above that of the other so that the canopies cannot be considered to be contiguous (e.g. date trees overlapping pomegranate trees at an oasis); and • border crops, where tall crops such as windbreaks border fields of shorter crops, or high trees border a field crop. 10. Under all conditions when combining crop coefficients for multiple crops, Kc should be constrained by this upper bound (Kc ≤ Kc max).

The type and condition of the ground surface during non-growing periods largely influences the range for ETc. text: In recent decades, research has produced a variety of strategies, methods, and technologies to reduce non-beneficial water use on farms for adaptation to the rising occurrence of water scarcity, agricultural droughts, and multi-sectoral rivalry for water, all which are increased by climate change. Adopting consumptive water-saving practices (WSET), i.e. that refer to ETc act requires accurate determination of crop water requirements using the FAO56 methods (Kc ETo) under various water availability and management techniques, as described in the previous chapters. However, the non-consumptive water-saving practices (WSDP+RO), that refer to controlling deep percolation (DP) and runoff (RO) at farm and off-farm, generally originate WSDP+RO > WSET. Both DP and RO refer to excess irrigation water applied relative to ETc and to limitations of the irrigation technologies and of the irrigators. In fact, water-saving practices must base not only on well-known net crop irrigation requirements but also on the availability of appropriate irrigation technologies and management. This section, therefore, outlines ideas and methods for reducing non-beneficial consumptive and non-consumptive water u

text: also on the availability of appropriate irrigation technologies and management. This section, therefore, outlines ideas and methods for reducing non-beneficial consumptive and non-consumptive water use, mainly referring to ET, DP and RO (NBWUET and NBWUDP+RO) while maintaining high crop water productivity on farms. These achievements tipically require maintaining high levels of water use for transpiration and managing the irrigation systems targeting ETc. In particular, this section describes water-saving routines linked to irrigation scheduling and management for irrigation systems, crop and soil management, mulching, remote sensing techniques, plant conditioners, and micro-climate adaptation. Controlling non-beneficial off- farm water use and non-consumptive farm water use imply different management and technological issues not dealt with in FAO56 but that are closely associated with the on-farm water management techniques and practices previously referred to and described hereafter. Off-farm reductions in water consumption include the adoption of modernized irrigation water collection, transport and distribution to farms and fields, and the use of automation for improving those related functions not described herein. All of these practices require an assessment of the local and regional hydrology to determine their overall impacts on reductions in water use. It is important to distinguish between water “use” and water “consumption” when assessing impacts of irrigation on the fresh water resource. Water consumption is the conversion of liquid water to vapour via the ET process, while the term water use describes the total extraction of water from the environment and used as irrigation water. Water use includes both the consumed part of the extracted water and the non-consumed part. In other words, water use consists of the consumptive use and the non-consumed part, that remains on the land surface but does not infiltrate into the irrigated field, and that stored below the surface. The first is runoff and the second is deep percolation as referred to before. If the non-consumed component flows back to a surface stream or to an underlying aquifer, then it remai

text: below the surface. The first is runoff and the second is deep percolation as referred to before. If the non-consumed component flows back to a surface stream or to an underlying aquifer, then it remains as part of the freshwater system and is available for later reuse. However, if the non-consumed component flows into a saline sink such as the ocean or brackish ground water, then it is no longer part of the freshwater system and is considered to be consumed. What is commonly considered to be “water savings’ is the difference between the common total water use, beneficial or not, and the water use when the irrigator manages water to avoid excess ET, or DP or RO. 10. As there is a strong relation between crop transpiration (Tc) and CO2 assimilation (gas exchange through stomata), higher Ya is achieved at the expense of more water transpired, mainly when aiming at little or no water stress. Chapter 8 develops the bases for irrigation scheduling and describes yield-water computations. Practical issues for determining crop coefficients under field practices and management Under conditions of water scarcity, the objective of irrigation management may be to optimize crop water productivity (WPET), i.e. the marketable yield per unit of water consumed if such a solution is economically appropriate. This involves knowing the economic water productivity ratio (EWPR), which is the ratio of the value of the marketable yield to the unit cost of water applied. Limited deficit irrigation (DI) is specifically introduced into the irrigation practice to allow some degree of crop water stress and Ya reduction, with a goal to reduce soil evaporation (Es) and water and chemical losses, whilst maintaining transpiration at levels that produce economically viable yields. Deficit irrigation can be considered to be a water-saving strategy where soil water depletion in the root zone goes below the optimum yield threshold and therefore transpiration decreases. Irrigation is applied up to a certain level below field capacity so that occasional rainfall can replenish the soil water storage capacity. Less frequent irrigation can reduce evaporation from the soil surface. However, the uneven distribution of rainfall and variable weather conditions pose a risk that may lead to Ya losses larger than desired or planned. To be a sustainable practice, reduction of water consumption in deficit irrigation should be proportionally higher than the reduction in Ya, so that WPET (kg m-3) is optimized, and EWPR is always p

To be a sustainable practice, reduction of water consumption in deficit irrigation should be proportionally higher than the reduction in Ya, so that WPET (kg m-3) is optimized, and EWPR is always positive (above the economic feasibility threshold, EWPR>1.0). Published research has provided inconsistent evidence on performance of deficit irrigation as a water-saving and economic strategy. In general, during years of water shortage, farmers may choose to adopt deficit irrigation schedules for their less profitable and more water-stress tolerant crops. To be economically viable, the cost of reduction of water use should be higher than the cost of reduction of the market value of Ya. This may be difficult to achieve or manage, depending on the degree of deficits. Therefore, deficit irrigation is not always the preferred option by farmers due to the increased risk of both Ya and monetary losses. Reducing the irrigated area may be a preferred solution, e.g. decreasing the irrigable area having annual crops in favour of watering of perennial crops. However, exceptions include the adoption of eustress in perennial crops where lower Ya results in better quality fruit and higher profits,

However, exceptions include the adoption of eustress in perennial crops where lower Ya results in better quality fruit and higher profits, as for grapevine where beneficial effects such as decreased berry size or increased sugar content may lead to great benefit since wine quality may be improved. Deficit irrigation can be implemented by applying a fixed water reduction strategy throughout the cropping season or targeted to some non-critical phenological stages in relation to water stress. Two main types of DI may be considered: • regulated deficit irrigation (RDI) that targets certain phenological stages during which plants are less sensitive to water stress; • partial root-zone drying (PRD), mostly used in fruit trees and vine crops, which targets the production of the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA), which reduces leaf expansion and stomatal conductance by stressing one portion of the roots, whilst the other portion of the roots sustains transpiration. This approach has been successfully applied to vegetable, field and tree crops and respective indicative parameters are tabulated in Chapter 9 to ease its application. Soil additives and conditioners are materials used to increase the soil water and nutrient retention capacity or to reduce Es. Many of these practices affect particularly the topsoil, which is the most dynamic soil layer in terms of mass and energy exchanges and may therefore impact Kc by decreasing Ke. Soil evaporation is site-specific depending upon climate through ETo, the frequency of soil wetting, the use of mulches, and the fraction of ground shadowed by the canopy, which depends upon the crop density and the crop growth stage. Es can be quantified through the partitioning of ET for the considered crop, namely using the dual Kc approach. Es is limited by the shading of the crop canopy, which corresponds to limitations imposed to the available energy for evaporation at the soil surface. This approach is valid for all irrigation methods that wet the soil surface and is in proportion to the wetted fraction, as occurs for furrow irrigation, particularly, when alternate furrows are adopted. As previously described in the current chapter, mulching is an old practice of covering the soil surface to reduce soil evaporation and surface runoff, regulate soil temperature, suppress weeds, improve soil health, and therefore improve crop growth. Different materials can be used for mulching, such as bark chips, straw, grass or other plant material, stones or plastic sheets, and humic substances. A wide variety of environmental and management factors have been reported in literature rel

A wide variety of environmental and management factors have been reported in literature relative to the complex crop growth response to various types of mulch. Effects of mulches are greater at earlier crop stages, when the soil is yet bare or only partially covered by the crop canopy. As a result, those are periods when crop coefficients greatly can vary with the frequency of wettings and soil wetness. Kc can be estimated according to the previous mulching section of this chapter. Only used in high-tech farming, plant conditioners include anti-transpirants, bio- stimulants and plant growth regulators. They are mainly applied to regulate harvesting dates of market produces, and to mitigate effects of environmental stresses. Although plant conditioners do not directly reduce NBWUET, they affect Tc or the Tc/ETc ratio and, therefore, their effects need to be considered when estimating total water consumption and in implementing irrigation scheduling. They may affect soil evaporation when plant conditioners decrease (or increase) the crop cover fraction due to their effects on plants. Anti-transpirants may act by reducing stomatal conductance and then the reduced Kcb may be assessed using the Fr factor described in the A&P approach (Chapter 9). These types of conditioners may become more and more prevalent in the future as research develops means to reduce transpiration from plants while sustaining inflow of carbon dioxide. 10. A typical case is sheltered or protected cultivation. However, as it happens with tunnels, the FAO PM-ETo does not apply since the aerodynamic conditions are changed and do not respect the Penman-Monteith assumptions.
