Windbreaks, such as trees, may mitigate extreme winds and affect micro-climatic variables such as net radiation (by increased shading), temperature, humidity, heat and evaporation fluxes resulting in changes in evaporative demands and water vapour fluxes. The effects of tree windbreaks depend on surface roughness, height, orientation and porosity. Warmer, more humid and less windy conditions usually occur in the protected crop areas. Lower wind speed and more humid conditions reduce vapor pressure deficit and crop ET, mostly without decreasing dry matter assimilation. Reduction of sensible heat fluxes and surface resistances, on the other hand, would most likely favor transpiration and dry matter assimilation. Higher Ya can therefore be expected in sheltered areas except when crops compete for resources with the windbreak plants (e.g. competition for water and nutrients). Generally, the trees in windbreaks are more tolerant of water shortage than agricultural crops and therefore can be irrigated less or not at all. Partial stomatal closure of the windbreak tree

Partial stomatal closure of the windbreak trees will cause a larger proportion of total available energy to be transformed into sensible heat rather than into evapotranspiration and total water consumption. As a result, total ET over large area of windbreaks and agriculture can be reduced. Irrigation methods can be broadly classified as surface, sprinkler and micro-irrigation. This section focuses on water-saving practices that are typical for each irrigation method and applicable on farms. It should be born in mind that costs and benefits play a major role when assessing respective water-saving issues because economic returns of irrigation tend to decrease when water-saving practices are adopted. Water consumption and use under different irrigation methods show sometimes contrasting outcomes, depending on the type of crop, canopy cover, soil properties (mainly relative to infiltration), land slope, irrigation wetted area, and irrigation management. Surface irrigation systems can have high performance when precise laser levelling

Surface irrigation systems can have high performance when precise laser levelling is adopted, inflow rates are adequate and non-erosive, and discharge applications are well controlled. These rules apply to either basin, border or furrow irrigation. Precise land levelling for basin, furrow and border irrigation is usually fundamental for efficient application with surface irrigation methods. When applied water creates ponds on the land surface before infiltrating into the soil, it not only leads to increased evaporation losses but decreases distribution uniformity (DU) of the infiltrated water. As a result, there will be parts of the field receiving less and parts receiving excessive water. If only the average depletion is replaced, then field-average ET will be decreased due to water stress on the under-irrigated portion of the field and field-average yields will decrease. To compensate for the less irrigated zones where the crop experiences stress, the farmer may tend to apply water in excess, thus promoting high deep percolation. Several authors reported that adop

Several authors reported that adopting precision land levelling in basin irrigation with controlled inflow rates and respective application time duration, reduced water application by nearly 40 percent relative to using less cared applications. However, the overall water consumption (evaporation and transpiration) may be similar but the cumulative soil evaporation may be less because the land surface is then usually wetted less frequently and transpiration increases because the canopy is increased and Es is reduced. Equipment for precise control of applied flow rates and volumes is rare where surface irrigation is traditional. The use of hand held equipment is not precise in control and largely depends upon the ability of the irrigant, which is another cause of non-uniformity of infiltrated volumes and, consequently, another reason why farmers may tend to apply excess water. In fact, the lack of precision control equipment makes it difficult to adopt precise scheduling in terms of managing discharge rates and volumes.

Basins are surrounded by soil bunds that avoid RO. This water plays a large role: providing for crop ET, controlling impacts of temperature on the crop and controlling weed growth. When land levelling is improved, the flooding depth may be reduced to about 5 cm, which may decrease deep percolation (DP). When the climate is favourable, intermittent (nearly daily) flooding may be practiced with the soil water kept near saturation, thereby further decreasing DP. When infrequent irrigation by surface, sprinkler or micro-irrigation is practised with aerobic rice production, both DP and Es may decrease, however depending upon soil and land surface conditions. The former includes portable and solid set systems and side roll. Continuous moving wheeled laterals are automated and include center-pivots, linear-move systems, travelling gun sprinklers and side-move systems. A primary objective of sprinkler systems is high water distribution uniformity throughout the irrigated field. Thus, potential water-saving practices aim at maintaining high DU when adopting sprinkler flow rates that favour water infiltration, spacing among sprinklers that provide for a good distribution

Thus, potential water-saving practices aim at maintaining high DU when adopting sprinkler flow rates that favour water infiltration, spacing among sprinklers that provide for a good distribution of water throughout the field, low variability of pressure and discharge if the field is sloping, system maintenance and design for controlling wind effects. If irrigation scheduling is appropriate in terms of the crop and soil water contents dynamics, these characteristics lead to high ratios of requirement to water applied, i.e., water application efficiencies. Sprinkler systems perform best when the soil infiltration is high, and wind speed is low. Sprinkler system design, mainly referring to the selection of sprinklers sizes and spacing, pressure, flow rates, water application depths and diameters of piping, is fundamental to ensure uniform distribution of pressure and flow rates, and to reduce evaporative losses. 10. Because water applied by large sprinkler systems wets the entire ground surface, non-beneficial consumption of water can be substantial under high wind and high evaporative demand of the atmosphere. Wind-induced evaporation of spray may be highest when drops are small, and when the canopy cover is low and risers are high above the ground surface. Evaporation of spray can be reduced by placing nozzles closer to or even inside the plant canopy, using larger drop sizes and attempting to irrigate when wind speeds are low. Modern sprinkler systems, such as center-pivot and linear moving laterals, are often designed to apply small irrigation depths to avoid runoff. As a result, they must irrigate more frequently, thereby increasing total evaporation losses from soil. The more frequent irrigation reduces the risk of crop stress, but at the expense of increased Es. The dual Kc procedure can be used to estimate the increases in Ke and Es under frequent irrigation. Micro-irrigation systems include high-tech methods having large capital and maintenance investment. Systems are low-pressure and include surface and subsurface drip irrigation for row crops and orchards, micro-sprinklers and micro-sprayers for horticulture and under- tree irrigation, and bubblers for orchards. These irrigation systems wet a limited portion of the ground, targeting the crop root zone, mainly in case of orchards and vines. The limited wetting of the surface reduces the soil evaporation impact due to high frequency irrigation, thus providing for high WSET by reducing NBWUET. Achieving good performance with micro-irrigation systems requires good design, which complexity may be overcome using decision support and design models. WS practices resulting from good design aim at improving water application control, the emission uniformity (EU), and the management of irrigation, as well as automation and control. The benefits of drip irrigation compared to surface and sprinkler irrigation include reduced water application, controlled operational water losses, less labour, low or no runoff and reduced energy consumption and pumping costs per unit area, as well as improved management of water, fertilization and pesticides for a range of high-profit crops. Micro- sprinklers and micro-sprayers have similar benefits, but the wetting pattern is wider and may be affected by wind. However, for under-tree irrigation, wind drift and Es may be less than for field crops. Despite advantages, managing drip or micro-spray irrigation systems for peak performance is very demanding, including when automation is adopted. High-tech micro-irrigation methods may not be economically feasible under all conditions since, for field crops, economic returns tend to decrease when more precision water-saving techniques are adopted. Water can be easily applied near the root zone of tree and vine crops, and it may be easier to apply deficit irrigation, in particular partial root-zone drying. Soil evaporation is controlled because the soil is only partially wetted near the crops, and often under the shadow of the crop canopy. When subsurface drip is applied, ground surface wetting occurs only by capillarity from the buried emitters. Drip irrigation, and border and basin irrigation, have advantages over sprinkler systems in saline environments by avoiding the wetting of the plant canopy. Drip irrigation can have reduced accumulation of salts in the root zone due to near continuous irrigation and therefore better suitability for salt sensitive crops. text: Quite often data sets containing a weather variable Yi observed at a given station are incomplete due to short interruptions in observations. Interruptions can be due to a large number of causes, the most frequent being the breakage or malfunction of instruments during a certain time period. When data are missing, it may be appropriate to complete these data sets from observations Xi from another nearby and reliable station. However, to use portions of data set Xi to insert in data set Yi, both data sets Xi and Yi must be homogeneous. In other words, they need to represent the same conditions throughout time.  The procedure for completing data sets must be applied after a test for homogeneity and any needed correction for non-homogeneity have been performed. chapter: Chapter 10 — ETc under various crop management practices
section: Analysis Of The Homogeneity Of Data Series
locator: Chapter 10 — ETc under various crop management practices — Analysis Of The Homogeneity Of Data Series
text: Weather data collected at a given weather station during a period of several years may be non-homogeneous when the data presents a sudden change in its mean and variance in relation to the original values. This phenomenon may occur due to several causes, Annex 3: Statistical analysis of weather data sets 375 some of which are related to changes in instrumentation and observation practices, and others which relate to modification of the environmental conditions of the site, such as rapid urbanization or, on the contrary, perhaps development of irrigation in the area. Changes relative to data collection may be caused by: • change in grass vegetation cover, its watering and management; • change in location of the weather station, or in type of shelters; • significant change in type of vegetation surrounding the weather station; • change of observer and/or the timing of observations; and • deterioration of sensors, or poor management of instruments leading to the These changes cause observations made prior and after the change to belong to statistically different populations. Quite often, the occurrence of such changes and the dates when they occurred are not known, making it necessary

Quite often, the occurrence of such changes and the dates when they occurred are not known, making it necessary to access whether a given data set can be considered homogeneous and, if not, to identify the sub-data series and Procedures indicated hereafter are simple, well proven in practice and rely upon the statistical comparison of two data sets, one considered homogeneous and consisting of observations Xi performed in a nearby weather station, the other being the one under analysis and consisting of the observations Yi of the same weather variable (Tmax, Tmin, u2, RHmax, Rs, etc). Both sets Xi and Yi should be collected at two stations that are in the same climatic region, have the same time length of observations and presenting the same trends in time despite the space variability when short time scales (daily, or 10-day) are utilized. When relating two weather data sets from two weather stations, where the first is homogeneous, the data set of the second station can be considered homogeneous if their cumulative residuals from its linear regression with the first data set are not biased. Its methodologies have become integral to irrigation planning, agricultural water management, and policy development However, advancements in data science, sensor technology, and climate modeling—coupled with emerging challenges such as prolonged droughts and changing weather patterns—have made it essential to revisit and strengthen the technical foundations of this cornerstone publication. The revised FAO 56 responds directly to this need, integrating modern tools such as remote sensing, IoT applications, and enhanced energy balance methods to improve the precision, relevance, and accessibility of crop water estimation under current and future climate This updated edition not only builds on the scientific rigor and widespread adoption of the original guidelines but also transpiration introduces practical innovations tailored to regional realities, particularly in water-stressed environments.
